title: Of course there are rude people
hookLine: when offended, ask: could the world exist without shameless people? (Meditations 9.42)

lines: THE MOST BELIEVABLE THING IN THE WORLD.
OF COURSE THERE ARE RUDE PEOPLE.
cards: Somebody cuts you off in traffic, and you hear yourself say it: unbelievable. A man talks through the whole movie. Unbelievable.
A coworker takes credit for your idea in the meeting. Unbelievable! But is it?
Honestly, it's about the most believable thing in the world. It happens every day, everywhere, and has for as long as there have been people. Part of what stings isn't the rudeness.
It's the surprise, as if the world had broken a promise. Marcus, who dealt with a great many difficult people, had a cure for the surprise.

teach.h: COULD THERE BE NO SHAMELESS PEOPLE?

teach.b: When you're offended by someone's shameless behavior, Marcus writes, ask yourself right away, in George Long's words: "Is it possible, then, that shameless men should not be in the world? It is not possible."
So don't ask for the impossible. This person is simply one of the ones who have to exist. Say the same, he adds, about the dishonest person and the one who lets you down.
The moment you remember that such people must be in the world, you'll be kinder to each one. Marcus isn't excusing rudeness. He's taking away the shock, so you can respond instead of react.
Then a practical question: what quality has nature given you to meet this?

Against the unkind person, he says, gentleness, like an antidote. And one more turn, a bit uncomfortable: if someone let you down, ask whether the fault is partly yours for expecting what they were never going to give.
This is the same man who started his mornings telling himself: today I'll meet the meddling, the ungrateful, the arrogant. Not to be gloomy. To be ready.
It closes our cooked week well. Dig within for the good. Let the heat soften you.
The story on top, not the thing itself. Put the bitter cucumber down. Leave in time.
And when the rude person arrives, as they will: of course. Your line.

how: Readers of Marcus often use this passage, and the similar morning reflection in Book Two, to prepare for difficult people before the day begins, so that rudeness brings less shock and more patience.

o: a sharp reply that puts a rude person in place
gentleness, the cure Marcus sets against unkindness
a poison you give back to whoever hurt you

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: they have to exist in the world
I'll meet the meddling and ungrateful

s: he isn't excusing it. he takes away the surprise so you can respond, not react.
Marcus says gentleness is nature's antidote to unkindness
he asks what quality you've been given to meet this, and names gentleness.

if someone let you down, ask whether you expected what they'd never give.

games.q: you're Marcus. someone at court has behaved shamelessly, and you're offended. what do you ask yourself first?
o: is a world without shameless people possible?
why does this always happen to me?
games.why: it is not possible, he answers. so don't ask for the impossible; this is one of the ones who must exist.

practice: Picture a moment where someone might be rude: the commute, a meeting, a phone call, the checkout line. Let it happen in your mind, feel the old flash of surprise, and say inside: of course.
Then picture yourself meeting it with a little gentleness.

wordCard.voice: Antidote. Marcus's word for gentleness, met against someone's rudeness, so you respond instead of react. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: shameless, without a sense of shame. Marcus's word for the people who offend us.

carryVoice: Your line: of course. That closes a whole week of being cooked. Rest well.

sources.q: Is it possible, then, that shameless men should not be in the world? It is not possible.
